title: Text Types and Their Features
summary: Fiction and non-fiction, every genre you can meet in the reading papers with its purpose and features, and how to answer “name the text type” and “give two features” questions.

blocks.text: Every reading text in Checkpoint 8 belongs to a **text type** (also called a genre). Paper 1 always gives you **non-fiction** (real information, real people, real events). Paper 2 always gives you **fiction** (an extract from a novel or short story). If you can recognise the text type quickly, you already know what the writer is trying to do, how the text will be organised and which features the examiner expects you to spot. This page gives you every genre you need, the features of each one, and a method for the questions that ask you to name a text type or give its features.

blocks.title: How this topic is tested
items: Name the text type: “What type of text is this?” or “Tick the text type that best describes paragraph 2.”
Give features: “Give two features that show this is a review.” / “Tick two features of a newspaper report used in the text.”
Formal or informal: “Give two features that make Text A formal.”
Compare two texts: when the insert has a Text A and a Text B, you may be asked for one feature they share and one way they are different.
Purpose links: a text-type question often sits next to a purpose question (inform, persuade, entertain…). See the page on purpose and viewpoint.
These questions are usually short (1-2 marks each), so they are quick marks if you know your features.

blocks.text: 1. Fiction or non-fiction?

Before you name a genre, decide which family the text belongs to. The one-line test: **if the writer’s job is to report what really happened or what is really true, it is non-fiction. If the writer’s job is to invent what could happen, it is fiction** — even when it is set in a real place.

rows: Based on
Facts, real life, real people and events
The writer’s imagination
Main purposes
To inform, explain, persuade, argue, advise, instruct, describe, recount
To entertain, to make the reader feel, to explore an idea or theme
People in it
Real people (named experts, witnesses, the writer)
Invented characters
Typical layout
Headings, sub-headings, bullet points, dates, captions, sign-offs
Paragraphs of narrative and dialogue · chapters
Typical language
Facts, statistics, quotations from experts, opinions, technical words
Description, dialogue, figurative language, suspense
Examples
Biography, article, report, leaflet, review, letter, blog, speech
Adventure, mystery, fantasy, science fiction, realistic fiction, fable

blocks.title: Tricky cases
items: A **historical novel** about a real war is still **fiction**: the characters and their conversations are invented.
A **travel article** uses beautiful description like a story, but it is **non-fiction**: the writer really went there.
An **autobiography** can read like a story (dialogue, suspense), but it is **non-fiction**: the events really happened to the writer.
A newspaper report about a story-writing competition is **non-fiction**, even though the winning story it mentions is fiction.

blocks.text: 2. What counts as a “feature”?
A feature is something you can **point to** in the text. There are two kinds. When a question says “give two features”, the safest answers name the feature **and** give a short example from the text.

rows: Language features (how it is written)

first person “I” · third person “he/she” · past tense · present tense · imperative verbs (“Mix…”, “Book now”) · time connectives (“First”, “After that”) · facts and statistics · opinions · quotations from experts or witnesses · rhetorical questions · direct address (“you”) · emotive language · formal vocabulary · informal language/slang/contractions · technical vocabulary · descriptive language and imagery
Layout / organisational features (how it looks)

headline · title · sub-headings · byline (writer’s name) · date · bullet points · numbered steps · paragraphs organised by topic or by time · captions · fact box · contact details · greeting and sign-off · star rating · subject line · slogan

blocks.title: A feature is not a topic
blocks.text: “It talks about dogs” is not a feature. “It uses technical vocabulary such as ‘canine’ and ‘breed’” is a feature. Always describe **how** the text is written or laid out, not **what** it is about.
3. All non-fiction genres and their features

Learn this table well. The left column is the genre, the middle is why people write it, and the right column lists the features that prove it. In the exam you only need two features, but knowing four or five gives you choice.

rows: Autobiography
To tell the story of the writer’s own life

First person (I, my) · past tense · covers a long period of the writer’s life, usually in time order · the writer’s feelings and reflections (“Looking back, I realise…”) · real names, dates and places
Memoir
To tell about one important period or experience of the writer’s life
First person · past tense · focuses on one time or theme · strong feelings and reflection · sensory description
Biography
To tell the story of another person’s life

Third person (he, she) · past tense · usually chronological (birth → achievements → later life) · facts, dates, places · quotations from the person or people who knew them · fairly formal, balanced tone
Recount
To retell events in the order they happened
Opening that tells who, what, where, when · past tense · time connectives (first, later, finally) · usually first person · specific details · ending with a personal comment
Diary / journal
To record the writer’s own day and feelings privately
Date at the top · “Dear Diary” (optional) · first person · past tense for events, present for feelings · informal, chatty · honest emotions · exclamations and questions to self
Letter (formal)
To complain, request, apply, inform or persuade someone official

Addresses and date · “Dear Sir or Madam” / “Dear Mrs Hassan” · clear reason for writing in paragraph 1 · formal vocabulary · no contractions · polite requests · “Yours faithfully” (name unknown) / “Yours sincerely” (name known)
Letter (informal)
To share news or feelings with a friend or relative
“Dear + first name,” · friendly, chatty tone · contractions (I’m, can’t) · questions to the reader · personal news · informal sign-off (“Love,” / “Best wishes,”)
Email
To communicate quickly, formally or informally
To / From / Subject line · greeting · short paragraphs · purpose stated early · sign-off · tone depends on reader (formal to a manager, informal to a friend)
Blog
To share experiences, opinions or advice online
Title and date · first person · chatty, personal voice · direct address (“Have you ever…?”) · opinions · humour · sometimes links, comments or hashtags · can be updated in posts
Magazine / feature article
To inform and entertain (sometimes persuade) readers about a topic
Catchy headline · strapline or sub-headings · engaging opening hook · mixture of facts and opinions · quotations · direct address · lively vocabulary · conclusion that returns to the opening idea
Newspaper report
To inform readers about a recent real event

Headline (often present tense, short) · byline · opening paragraph answers who, what, where, when (why/how) · third person · past tense · quotations from witnesses or officials · most important facts first · formal, factual tone · photograph and caption
Non-chronological report
To give facts about a subject organised by topic, not time

Title · introduction that classifies the subject · sub-headings (appearance, habitat, diet…) · present tense · third person · formal, impersonal tone · technical vocabulary · facts and statistics · diagrams and fact boxes
Information / explanation text
To explain how or why something happens
Present tense · cause-and-effect connectives (because, as a result, therefore) · technical vocabulary, sometimes explained · diagrams · logical sequence
Persuasive text (speech, advert, letter, article)
To make the reader think or act in a certain way

Strong one-sided opinion · emotive language · rhetorical questions · direct address (you) · inclusive “we/us” · rule of three · repetition · exaggeration · statistics chosen to support the writer · call to action with imperatives (“Join us today!”)
Argument (argumentative text)
To prove one point of view using reasons and evidence

Clear position stated early · each paragraph gives one reason with evidence · logical connectives (therefore, this shows, furthermore) · the opposite view is mentioned and then answered (counter-argument) · confident, formal tone · conclusion repeats the position
Discursive / balanced argument
To discuss both sides of an issue fairly

Introduction presents the issue · arguments for and against given equal space · connectives of contrast (however, on the other hand) · cautious words (may, might, perhaps) · writer’s own view only in the conclusion
Speech
To speak to and move a live audience
Greeting to the audience · direct address · rhetorical questions · repetition and rule of three · short sentences for impact · signposting (firstly, finally) · memorable ending or call to action
Review
To judge a film, book, product, place or event and recommend it (or not)

Title or name of what is reviewed · short summary without spoilers · first-person opinion · evaluative adjectives (gripping, disappointing) · comparatives and superlatives · good and bad points with examples · final verdict, recommendation or star rating
Leaflet / brochure
To inform or persuade the reader quickly about one subject
Eye-catching title and slogan · sub-headings · bullet points · short sentences · direct address (you) · imperatives · persuasive adjectives · boxed key facts · contact details, prices, opening times
Travel writing
To describe a place and the writer’s journey so the reader can imagine it

First person · vivid description using the five senses · similes and metaphors · personal anecdotes · mixture of past (the journey) and present (what the place is like) · practical tips (how to get there, cost, best time)
Instructions / procedural text
To tell the reader how to do or make something

Title stating the goal (“How to…”) · list of equipment/ingredients · numbered steps in order · imperative verbs at the start (Cut, Stir, Press) · time connectives · short, precise sentences · no unnecessary description · diagrams
Advice text
To help the reader solve a problem or make a good choice

Direct address (you) · modal verbs (you should, you could, it might help to) · imperatives softened politely (Try to…) · sympathetic, reassuring tone · tips organised as points or paragraphs · often a question-and-answer format (problem page)

ما تكتبش موضوع النص على إنه feature. الـ feature هي طريقة الكتابة أو شكل الصفحة.

blocks.text: 4. Genres that students confuse
Many wrong answers come from mixing up two genres that look similar. Learn the one difference that separates each pair.

rows: Biography vs autobiography
Biography = someone else’s life, third person (she). Autobiography = the writer’s own life, first person (I).
Autobiography vs memoir
Autobiography covers most of a life. Memoir focuses on one period or experience.
Recount vs diary
Both retell events in order. A diary is dated, private and full of feelings. A recount is written for a reader and is more organised.
Diary vs blog
A diary is private. A blog is public and talks to readers (“What do you think?”).
Newspaper report vs magazine article
A report gives the facts of a recent event objectively. An article explores a topic, mixes facts with opinion and tries to entertain.
Recount vs non-chronological report
A recount is organised by time (what happened next). A non-chronological report is organised by topic (habitat, diet, appearance).
Persuasive vs argument
Persuasive writing mainly uses emotion (emotive words, direct appeals). An argument mainly uses logic and evidence and answers the other side.
Argument vs discursive
An argument takes one side from the start. A discursive text gives both sides fairly and decides only at the end.
Instructions vs advice
Instructions give exact steps in order with commands (Press the button). Advice gives suggestions with modal verbs (You could try…).
Review vs article
A review judges one thing and ends with a verdict or rating. An article discusses a wider topic.
Leaflet vs article
A leaflet is short, broken into boxes and bullet points, with contact details. An article is continuous paragraphs.
Travel writing vs non-chronological report
Travel writing is personal (I, feelings, the journey). A report about a country is impersonal (third person, facts by topic).
Letter vs email
An email has a subject line and is usually shorter. A formal letter has addresses and “Yours sincerely/faithfully”.

blocks.text: 5. Formal and informal features
A common question asks for features that make a text **formal** (or informal). Use this table. Remember to quote an example for each feature you give.

rows: Full forms: “do not”, “it is”
Contractions: “don’t”, “it’s”
Standard English and precise vocabulary: “purchase”, “assist”, “numerous”
Slang and chatty words: “loads of”, “awesome”, “stuff”
Third person and impersonal phrases: “It is recommended that…”
First and second person: “I reckon you’ll love it”
Passive voice: “The bridge was opened in 2019.”
Active, personal voice: “They opened the bridge ages ago.”
Polite, distant greetings and sign-offs: “Dear Sir or Madam”, “Yours faithfully”
Friendly greetings: “Hi Omar,” and “Cheers,”
Longer, complex sentences
Short sentences, questions, exclamation marks, humour
Facts, statistics, named experts
Personal anecdotes and feelings

blocks.text: 6. Fiction genres and their features

Paper 2 extracts come from stories and novels. You may be asked what kind of story the extract seems to come from, or which features show this. Look at the **setting**, the **characters** and the **kind of events**.

rows: Adventure
Remote or dangerous places: seas, jungles, mountains, deserts
Brave, resourceful hero · companions · enemies
Journey or quest · physical danger · fast pace · short action sentences · cliffhangers
Realistic fiction
Ordinary places today: home, school, a town
Believable people with everyday problems
Events that could really happen · friendship, family, growing up · feelings and relationships · no magic
Fantasy
Invented worlds or a hidden magical side of our world
Wizards, magical creatures, a chosen hero
Magic with its own rules · good against evil · quests · invented names and places
Science fiction
The future, space, other planets, laboratories
Scientists, astronauts, robots, aliens
Advanced technology · “What if…?” ideas · technical-sounding vocabulary · questions about the future
Dystopian
A future society that has gone wrong
A hero who questions the rules
Control, surveillance, strict rules · fear · rebellion · a warning about the present
Mystery
Often a closed place: a house, a village, a train
Detective or curious young person · suspects
A puzzle or secret · clues · red herrings · suspense · a final reveal
Crime
Cities, police stations, courtrooms
Criminals, police, victims
A crime and its investigation · realistic procedure · consequences
Horror / Gothic
Dark, isolated places: old houses, forests at night, storms
Victims, ghosts, monsters, a threatening unknown
Fear and dread · eerie atmosphere · pathetic fallacy · sounds in the dark · build-up of tension · shock
Historical fiction
A real period in the past
Invented characters, sometimes beside real people
Period details (clothes, transport, speech) · real events in the background
Myth
The ancient world, the heavens, the underworld
Gods, goddesses, heroes, monsters
Explains how something began (the seasons, thunder) · grand events · supernatural powers
Legend
A real historical place and time
A hero who may have really lived
Based on a real person or event but exaggerated over time · bravery · passed down through generations
Fable
Very simple: a field, a forest, a river bank
Animals that talk and act like people
Very short · each animal shows a human quality (the proud lion) · a moral at the end
Fairy tale
Castles, forests, kingdoms, “once upon a time”
Princes, princesses, witches, talking animals
Magic objects · clear good and evil · patterns of three · happy ending
Folktale
A village “long ago”
Ordinary people, often without names (a poor farmer)
Passed down by word of mouth · simple plot · teaches a value
Comedy / humorous fiction
Usually everyday places
Clumsy or exaggerated characters
Funny misunderstandings · exaggeration · wordplay · light-hearted ending
Play script (drama)
Given in stage directions
Shown only through what they say and do
Character names before lines · stage directions in brackets or italics · no narrator

blocks.text: Whatever the genre, every story extract also has the **features of narrative**: a narrator (first person “I” or third person “he/she”), a setting, characters, dialogue in inverted commas, description, and a plot that builds towards a problem or a turning point. If a question asks for “two features of a story”, these are safe answers.
7. Method: name the text type and prove it

items: **Look at the layout first.** Headline? Bullet points? Date? Numbered steps? “Dear…”? A subject line? Layout often gives the answer in five seconds.

**Check the person and tense.** I/past = autobiography, recount, diary. She/past = biography, report. Present/third person = non-chronological report or information text. Imperatives = instructions or leaflet.
**Ask what the writer wants.** To inform, persuade, advise, entertain? The purpose narrows the genre.
**Name the genre exactly.** Write “a newspaper report”, not “an informative text”, unless the question asks for the purpose.
**Prove it with features.** For each mark: name the feature + quote a short example. One feature per mark, clearly separated.

blocks.text: 8. Worked examples
**Example 1.** Read this extract:

“FLOODS CLOSE COASTAL ROAD. Residents of Ras El Bar were moved to safety yesterday after heavy rain flooded the main coastal road. ‘The water rose faster than anyone expected,’ said local official Karim Fawzy. The road will remain closed until Friday.”
**Question:** What type of text is this? Give two features that show this. (2 marks)

**Answer:** It is a newspaper report. It has a short headline in capital letters, “FLOODS CLOSE COASTAL ROAD”, and it includes a quotation from an official: “The water rose faster than anyone expected”.

**Why it works:** the genre is named exactly, and each feature is named and then proved with a quotation. Other correct features: the opening sentence tells who, what, where and when · it is written in the past tense and the third person.
**Example 2.** Read this extract:

“Feeling anxious before exams? You are not alone. Try breaking your revision into short sessions with breaks in between. It might also help to talk to someone you trust. Remember: a good night’s sleep is worth more than an extra hour of panic.”
**Question:** Give two features of advice writing used in this text. (2 marks)
**Answer:** It speaks directly to the reader with a question, “Feeling anxious before exams?”. It uses gentle suggestions with modal verbs, “It might also help to talk to someone you trust”.
**Why it works:** “direct address” and “modal verbs” are features, not topics. A weak answer would say “it is about exams”, which earns nothing.
**Example 3 (comparing two texts).** Text A is a leaflet for a science museum. Text B is a student’s diary entry about visiting the same museum.
**Question:** Give one way the two texts are similar and one way they are different. (2 marks)

**Answer:** Similar: both describe the museum’s exhibits, for example the planetarium. Different: Text A is formal and uses bullet points and opening times, while Text B is informal and uses the first person to share feelings, “I couldn’t stop smiling”.

blocks.title: Common traps
items: Giving the **purpose** when the question asks for the **text type** (“to persuade” is not a genre).
Writing “it has paragraphs”. Almost every text has paragraphs, so it proves nothing. Say how the paragraphs are organised (by time / by topic).
Writing two features in one long sentence so the examiner cannot separate them. Use two sentences.
Naming a feature that is **not** in this text. Only give features you can quote.
Calling a story “non-fiction” because it feels realistic, or calling travel writing “fiction” because it is descriptive.

blocks.title: خطأ بيضيّع درجات كتير
blocks.text: أول ما تشوف كلمة features في السؤال، اكتب الميزة باسمها الصحيح (headline, imperative verbs, first person, rhetorical question…) وبعدها مثال من النص بين علامتي تنصيص. ولو السؤال بيقارن بين Text A و Text B، لازم تذكر النصين الاتنين في إجابتك، مش نص واحد بس.
9. Practice questions
Each extract below is short and original. Answer in full sentences, then check.

items.q: “Born in a small village near Aswan in 1931, Hamid Ali taught himself to read by candlelight. By the age of twenty, he had opened the town’s first library.” What type of text is this? Give one feature that proves it.
items.a: A biography. It is written in the third person about someone else’s life (“he had opened the town’s first library”). It also gives dates (“in 1931”) and follows time order.

items.q: “I was seven when my family moved to Alexandria. I remember hating the noise at first. Later, the sea became the best friend I had.” Biography or autobiography? Explain.
items.a: Autobiography: the writer tells the story of their own life in the first person (“I was seven”, “my family”).

items.q: “1. Fill the pot with soil. 2. Push the seed two centimetres down. 3. Water gently every morning.” Name the text type and give two features.
items.a: Instructions. Features: numbered steps in order (“1.”, “2.”, “3.”) and imperative verbs at the start of each step (“Fill”, “Push”, “Water”).

items.q: “Sea turtles are reptiles that live in warm oceans. Diet: most adults eat seagrass. Lifespan: many live for over fifty years.” Name the text type and give two features.
items.a: A non-chronological report. It uses the present tense for general facts (“are reptiles”, “live”) and is organised by topic with sub-headings (“Diet”, “Lifespan”).

items.q: “Monday 4th March. What a disaster! I forgot my PE kit AGAIN and Mr Samir gave me that look. Tomorrow I’m packing my bag the night before. I mean it this time.” Name the text type and give two features.
items.a: A diary entry. It has a date at the top (“Monday 4th March”) and an informal, emotional first-person voice with exclamations (“What a disaster!”).

items.q: “Are you tired of boring weekends? Then come to the Green Valley Farm Festival! Pick fresh strawberries, meet friendly animals and taste homemade bread. Don’t miss out — book today!” Give two persuasive features.
items.a: A rhetorical question to the reader (“Are you tired of boring weekends?”) and an imperative call to action (“book today!”). Also accept: rule of three (“Pick…, meet…, taste…”), positive adjectives (“friendly”, “fresh”).

items.q: “Some people believe school should start later because teenagers need more sleep. On the other hand, a later start would mean finishing later in the afternoon.” Is this persuasive, argument or discursive writing? Explain.
items.a: Discursive (balanced): it presents both sides fairly and links them with the contrast connective “On the other hand”, without taking a side yet.

items.q: “The acting is superb, but the story drags in the middle. Overall, I would give it three stars and recommend it to anyone who enjoys slow, thoughtful films.” Name two features of a review.
items.a: A first-person opinion with evaluative words (“superb”, “drags”) and a final verdict with a rating and recommendation (“three stars”, “recommend it to anyone who…”).

items.q: “From: Laila Adel. Subject: Missing library book. Dear Mr Nabil, I am writing to explain why my book is late…” Name the text type and say whether it is formal or informal, with one reason.
items.a: An email (it has From and Subject lines). It is formal: it uses a polite greeting with a title, “Dear Mr Nabil”, and the full form “I am writing” instead of a contraction.

items.q: Give two features that make this sentence formal: “Visitors are requested not to feed the animals as this may cause them serious harm.”
items.a: The passive voice (“Visitors are requested”) and formal vocabulary with no contractions (“requested”, “may cause them serious harm”). It is also impersonal (no “I” or “you”).

items.q: “The ferry chugged into the harbour as the sun melted into the sea. I could smell grilled fish and hear fishermen shouting prices. Top tip: arrive before nine to beat the crowds.” Name the text type and give two features.
items.a: Travel writing. It uses sensory description (“smell grilled fish”, “hear fishermen shouting”) and gives practical advice to the reader (“Top tip: arrive before nine”). It is also written in the first person.

items.q: “The fox praised the crow’s beautiful voice. The crow opened its beak to sing, and the cheese fell straight into the fox’s mouth. Never trust a flatterer.” Name the fiction genre and give two features.
items.a: A fable. It has animals that behave like people (a fox and a crow who talk and think) and it ends with a moral (“Never trust a flatterer”).

items.q: “The airlock hissed open. Beyond it, the red dust of the third colony stretched to the horizon, and the dome’s computer announced that oxygen reserves were at nine per cent.” Which fiction genre is this? Give two clues.
items.a: Science fiction. Clues: advanced technology (“airlock”, “the dome’s computer”) and a setting on another planet or colony (“the red dust of the third colony”).

items.q: “Thunder shook the shutters of the empty house. Somewhere upstairs, a door creaked open by itself.” Which genre and which features?
items.a: Horror (or Gothic). It has a dark, isolated setting (“the empty house”), stormy weather that creates fear (pathetic fallacy, “Thunder shook the shutters”) and an unexplained, frightening event (“a door creaked open by itself”).

items.q: Text A is a newspaper report about a new metro line. Text B is a blog post by a commuter about her first ride. Give one difference in the way they are written.
items.a: Text A is written in the third person with a formal, factual tone and quotations from officials, while Text B is written in the first person with an informal, personal tone that shares the writer’s feelings.

items.q: Why is a novel about a real ancient battle, with invented soldiers as main characters, called fiction?
items.a: Because the main characters, their thoughts and their conversations are invented by the author. The real battle is only the background.

items.q: A student writes: “Two features of this leaflet are that it is about healthy eating and it is interesting.” Why does this score 0? Rewrite it.
items.a: Both are about the topic or the student’s opinion, not features. Better: “It uses sub-headings such as ‘Five a day’, and bullet points to list the tips.”
